questions.q: Culpable Homicide is defined under Section 100 of the BNS, which corresponds to which section of the old IPC?
o: Section 300
Section 299
Section 302
Section 304
questions.src: Section 100 BNS corresponds directly to Section 299 IPC -- the definition of culpable homicide.

questions.q: Murder is defined under Section 101 of the BNS, corresponding to which section of the old IPC?
o: Section 299
Section 300
Section 302
Section 304A
questions.src: Section 101 BNS corresponds to Section 300 IPC -- the definition of murder as an aggravated species of culpable homicide.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Culpable homicide is the genus, and murder is a species of it. Reason (R): All culpable homicide amounts to murder, and all murder amounts to culpable homicide. Which is correct?
o: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) correctly explains (A)
(A) is true, but (R) is FALSE -- not all culpable homicide amounts to murder, though all murder is culpable homicide
Both (A) and (R) are false
(A) is false, but (R) is true
questions.src: This is a classic genus-species trap: (A) is correct, but (R) wrongly claims the relationship works in both directions -- it does not.

questions.q: Under Section 101 BNS (Section 300 IPC), Exception 1 (Grave and Sudden Provocation) will NOT apply if:
o: The provocation was genuinely sudden and unexpected
The provocation was SELF-SOUGHT by the offender as an excuse for the killing
The offender had no time to plan the act
The victim was a stranger to the offender
questions.src: One of the key provisos to Exception 1 excludes self-sought or voluntarily provoked provocation used as a pretext.

questions.q: If grave and sudden provocation was given by something done by a public servant in the LAWFUL exercise of their power, Exception 1 to Murder:
o: Applies fully, reducing the offence to culpable homicide
Does NOT apply -- the killing remains MURDER
Applies only if the public servant was off-duty
Is irrelevant to the classification of the offence
questions.src: A specific proviso excludes provocation stemming from a public servant's lawful exercise of power -- Exception 1 fails in this scenario.

questions.q: Under Exception 2 to Murder (Exceeding the Right of Private Defence), the offender's act must be done:
o: With premeditation and intent to cause maximum harm
In GOOD FAITH, WITHOUT premeditation, and without intention of doing more harm than necessary
Only against a stranger, never a family member
Only in daylight hours
questions.src: Exception 2 requires good faith, absence of premeditation, and no intention to exceed necessary harm -- all three conditions must be met.

questions.q: Statement 1: An offender who was the ORIGINAL AGGRESSOR in a confrontation can generally still successfully claim Exception 2 (exceeding private defence). Statement 2: Exception 2 requires the private defence to have been genuinely exercised in good faith. Which is correct?
o: Both statements are true
Only Statement 1 is true
Only Statement 2 is true
Both statements are false
questions.src: Statement 1 is false -- an original aggressor generally cannot claim private defence at all, defeating Exception 2. Statement 2 correctly reflects the good-faith requirement.

questions.q: Under Exception 5 to Murder (Consent), for this exception to apply, the deceased must have been:
o: Any age, with any form of consent
ABOVE EIGHTEEN years of age, voluntarily consenting to the risk of death or to death itself
A close relative of the accused
Below eighteen years of age
questions.src: Exception 5 specifically requires the deceased to be above 18 and to have genuinely, voluntarily consented.

questions.q: Section 103(2) BNS, a GENUINELY NEW provision absent from the original IPC, punishes murder committed by:
o: A single individual acting alone
A GROUP OF FIVE OR MORE persons acting in concert on grounds like caste, race, community, or personal belief (mob lynching)
Only government officials
Only during a declared national emergency
questions.src: Section 103(2) is a new BNS provision specifically targeting group/mob-based murders motivated by identity-based grounds.

questions.q: In Mithu v. State of Punjab (1983), the Supreme Court struck down Section 303 IPC (mandatory death sentence for murder by a life-convict) for violating:
o: Only Article 19
Article 14 and Article 21
Only Article 32
Only Article 300A
questions.src: Mithu held mandatory death sentences with no judicial discretion violate both equality (Art 14) and life/personal liberty (Art 21).

questions.q: In Bachan Singh v. State of Punjab (1980), the Supreme Court established the "rarest of rare" doctrine, holding that:
o: Death sentence should be the default rule for all murder convictions
LIFE IMPRISONMENT is the rule for murder, and DEATH SENTENCE the exception, requiring special reasons
All murder convictions require exactly the same sentence
Judicial discretion in sentencing should be entirely eliminated
questions.src: Bachan Singh established that death sentences require special justification, with life imprisonment as the default rule.

questions.q: In Virsa Singh v. State of Punjab (1958), the Supreme Court clarified that for Section 101(c) BNS/Section 300(3) IPC to apply, the prosecution must prove:
o: The accused subjectively intended for the victim to die
The bodily injury inflicted was OBJECTIVELY SUFFICIENT, in the ordinary course of nature, to cause death
The accused had a documented motive for the killing
The victim survived for at least 24 hours after the injury
questions.src: Virsa Singh established an objective sufficiency test, not a subjective intent-to-kill requirement, for this specific murder clause.

questions.q: In K.M. Nanavati v. State of Maharashtra (1961), the Supreme Court held that the provocation in question was NOT "sudden" because:
o: The victim provoked the accused repeatedly over many years
There was a TIME GAP allowing the accused's passion to cool before the killing
The accused had no weapon available
The provocation occurred in a public place
questions.src: The time gap allowing for cooling of passion defeated the "sudden" element required for Exception 1 to apply, resulting in a murder conviction.

questions.q: Under the old IPC, Section 303 dealt with "Punishment for Murder by Life Convict." Under the NEW BNS, Section 303 deals with an entirely DIFFERENT offence:
o: Kidnapping
THEFT
Criminal conspiracy
Abetment of suicide
questions.src: A classic trap -- Section 303 has completely different meanings under IPC (murder by life convict, now struck down) versus BNS (theft). Never assume identical section numbers mean identical offences across the two codes.

questions.q: General Exceptions under BNS Chapter III include "Mistake of Fact" -- this excuses an act done by a person:
o: Under a mistake of LAW, regardless of good faith
Bound, or believing in good faith to be bound, by LAW to do it
Purely out of personal convenience
Only if the mistake benefited a third party
questions.src: Mistake of fact (not mistake of law) can excuse liability, where the person genuinely, reasonably believed they were legally bound/justified.

questions.q: Under Section 20 BNS (General Exceptions), a child UNDER 7 years of age has:
o: Full criminal liability like an adult
ABSOLUTE incapacity -- nothing done by them is an offence
Liability only for serious offences
Liability determined case-by-case with no fixed rule
questions.src: Section 20 creates an absolute, irrebuttable incapacity for children under 7.

questions.q: Abetment, under Chapter V BNS, may occur through which THREE means?
o: Only through direct physical participation
INSTIGATION, engaging in a CONSPIRACY (with an act/omission in pursuance), or INTENTIONALLY AIDING the commission of the offence
Only through written communication
Only if the abettor is present at the scene
questions.src: These are the three recognised means by which a person can abet an offence under the BNS abetment provisions.

questions.q: Under Criminal Conspiracy (Sections 61-62 BNS), for an agreement between two or more persons to constitute the offence, generally:
o: The mere agreement is ALWAYS sufficient regardless of the intended offence
The mere agreement suffices ONLY where the intended offence carries death/life imprisonment/2+ years rigorous imprisonment; OTHERWISE an overt act beyond the agreement is required
No agreement can ever constitute a criminal conspiracy
Only written agreements count as criminal conspiracy
questions.src: This nuanced rule distinguishes serious offences (mere agreement suffices) from lesser offences (an overt act beyond agreement is additionally required).

questions.q: Under Section 62 BNS (the general Attempt provision, corresponding to Section 511 IPC), where an attempted offence is NOT completed, the punishment may extend to:
o: The FULL maximum term for the completed offence
ONE-HALF of the longest term provided for the completed offence, or fine, or both
Double the maximum term as a deterrent
No punishment applies to mere attempts
questions.src: This is the precise numerical formula for general attempt liability -- up to half the maximum term for the completed offence.

questions.q: Assertion (A): BNS has 358 sections across 20 chapters. Reason (R): This represents a significant reduction from the IPC's 511 sections, reflecting consolidation of provisions and removal of obsolete/struck-down sections. Which is correct?
o: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) correctly explains (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) does not explain (A)
(A) is true, but (R) is false
(A) is false, but (R) is true
questions.src: Both statements are accurate, and the reduction genuinely reflects consolidation rather than a narrowing of substantive criminal law coverage.

questions.q: "Kidnapping" under BNS is governed by Section 137, corresponding to which IPC section?
o: Section 350
Section 359
Section 362
Section 378
questions.src: Section 137 BNS corresponds to Section 359 IPC on kidnapping.

questions.q: "Abduction" under BNS is governed by Section 138, corresponding to which IPC section?
o: Section 359
Section 362
Section 378
Section 383
questions.src: Section 138 BNS corresponds to Section 362 IPC on abduction, distinct from the kidnapping provision.

questions.q: In the general exceptions framework, "Necessity" excuses an act done:
o: For purely personal financial gain
In GOOD FAITH to prevent OTHER, greater harm to person or property
Only by government officials
Only when no alternative exists whatsoever, with no good faith requirement
questions.src: The necessity exception requires genuine good faith and a real purpose of avoiding greater harm, not a pretext.

questions.q: "Voluntary Intoxication," under the general exceptions framework, is generally treated as:
o: An automatic, complete defence to any criminal charge
NOT a defence generally, though it may be relevant to whether specific intent for certain offences was actually formed
Identical in legal effect to involuntary intoxication
A defence available only to first-time offenders
questions.src: Voluntary intoxication does not generally excuse criminal liability, though courts may consider it in assessing specific intent requirements for particular offences.

questions.q: "Criminal Force," under BNS Section 129 (corresponding to IPC Section 350), as distinguished from "Assault," involves:
o: Only the apprehension of force, not actual contact
The intentional USE of ACTUAL force on another person without consent
Only verbal threats with no physical component
A tort, not a criminal offence
questions.src: Criminal Force involves actual application of force, distinguished from Assault (mere apprehension of imminent force).

questions.q: Under the right of private defence framework (Sections 34-44 BNS), Section 37's restrictions include that the right:
o: Extends without limit to any amount of harm the defender chooses
NEVER extends to inflicting MORE HARM than necessary for the purpose of defence
Applies only to defence of property, never the body
Requires prior police permission before being exercised
questions.src: Section 37 caps the right of private defence, ensuring it never extends beyond what is genuinely necessary for the defensive purpose.

questions.q: Match the following murder-exception scenarios with their correct classification: (i) Offender exceeds private defence in good faith without premeditation (ii) Offender kills after provocation they themselves sought as a pretext (iii) Sudden fight without undue advantage (iv) Deceased, aged 20, voluntarily consented to the risk of death
o: (i)-Exception 2, (ii)-Exception 1 applies, (iii)-Exception 4, (iv)-Exception 5
(i)-Exception 2, (ii)-Exception 1 does NOT apply (self-sought), (iii)-Exception 4, (iv)-Exception 5
(i)-Exception 1, (ii)-Exception 2, (iii)-Exception 3, (iv)-Exception 4
(i)-Exception 5, (ii)-Exception 4, (iii)-Exception 3, (iv)-Exception 2
questions.src: Correctly matching: (i) exceeding private defence = Exception 2; (ii) self-sought provocation defeats Exception 1 entirely; (iii) sudden fight = Exception 4; (iv) valid adult consent = Exception 5.

questions.q: Under Section 105 BNS (Section 304 IPC, Punishment for Culpable Homicide Not Amounting to Murder), the punishment differs based on whether the act was done:
o: On a weekday versus a weekend
With the INTENTION of causing death/likely-fatal injury (higher punishment) versus mere KNOWLEDGE it was likely to cause death without such intention (lower punishment)
Indoors versus outdoors
By a first-time versus repeat offender only
questions.src: Section 105 BNS prescribes two distinct punishment tiers based on whether intention or mere knowledge was the operative mental element.

questions.q: "Grievous Hurt" under BNS (corresponding to IPC Section 320) includes categories such as:
o: Any momentary bodily discomfort, however minor
Emasculation, permanent privation of sight/hearing, fracture/dislocation of a bone, or hurt causing severe pain/inability to pursue ordinary activities for 20 days
Only hurt caused by a specifically named weapon
Only hurt resulting in immediate death
questions.src: Grievous Hurt is a specifically enumerated, more serious category of hurt than the ordinary threshold, covering these listed severe categories.

questions.q: Statement 1: Attempt to Murder (Section 109 BNS/Section 307 IPC) requires that death actually resulted from the accused's act. Statement 2: An attempt to murder can be punished even where the intended victim survives the attack. Which is correct?
o: Both statements are true
Only Statement 1 is true
Only Statement 2 is true
Both statements are false
questions.src: Statement 1 is false -- attempt to murder specifically does NOT require death to have occurred (if it did, the offence would be murder itself, not attempt). Statement 2 is correct -- the offence is complete even if the victim survives.
